\chapter{Courtesy}
\label{ch:ta-courtesy}
\hlchaptermodality{49}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can thank somebody warmly in Tamil, show respect, and wish them well.}

Complete TA-C49-many-thanks and say all five words in order.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[aṉbu]{\ta{அன்பு} (aṉbu) — affection}

\label{lesson:TA-C49-affection}



\begin{quote}
Before the new run of words: what did \emph{piṟaku} mean, and what did \emph{puṟappaḍu} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{அன்பு}}
\textbf{\ta{அன்பு}} (\emph{aṉbu}) — \textquotedblleft{}affection\textquotedblright{}.

This is the warm, ordinary love — for a family, for a friend, for a place. \emph{kādal} is the other kind, the one the poems are about, and Tamil keeps the two apart where English makes one word do both.

A letter opens \emph{aṉbuḷḷa}, \textquotedblleft{}dear\textquotedblright{}, which is literally 'having affection'. Put the endings you know on the stem and you get \emph{aṉbaṉ} and \emph{aṉbar}, somebody who loves — the same two endings, doing the same work, on new material.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first of five courtesies.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{aṉbu}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{aṉbu}, then \emph{aṉbuḷḷa}, and hear the stem stay put
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{அன்பு} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}affection\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[mariyādai]{\ta{மரியாதை} (mariyādai) — respect}

\label{lesson:TA-C49-respect}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{aṉbu} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{மரியாதை}}
\textbf{\ta{மரியாதை}} (\emph{mariyādai}) — \textquotedblleft{}respect\textquotedblright{}.

Sanskrit \emph{maryādā}, which started life as a boundary mark — the line at the edge of a field. Respect, in that picture, is knowing where the line runs and not stepping over it.

Tamil shows it in its endings as much as in its words. You have been doing it since \emph{nīṅgaḷ}, where the ending meant for many is aimed at one person on purpose: \emph{mariyādai} built out of shape rather than out of vocabulary.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two: what you feel, and what you show.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{mariyādai}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{aṉbu}, then \emph{mariyādai}, so the warm one and the formal one sit together
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{மரியாதை} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}respect\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[santōṣam]{\ta{சந்தோஷம்} (santōṣam) — gladness}

\label{lesson:TA-C49-gladness}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{mariyādai} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{சந்தோஷம்}}
\textbf{\ta{சந்தோஷம்}} (\emph{santōṣam}) — \textquotedblleft{}gladness\textquotedblright{}.

Sanskrit \emph{santoṣa}, 'contentment', sitting beside the native \emph{magiḻcci} you met when somebody was pleased to see you. Both are in daily use and neither has driven the other out — the same arrangement as \emph{nalam} and \emph{sugam}.

\emph{santōṣam} is what you reach for when you accept an invitation. On its own, in reply, it means \textquotedblleft{}gladly\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three, and the third one is an answer as much as a feeling.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{santōṣam}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{mariyādai}, then \emph{santōṣam}, and let the second one lift
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{சந்தோஷம்} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}gladness\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[vāḻttu]{\ta{வாழ்த்து} (vāḻttu) — a good wish}

\label{lesson:TA-C49-good-wish}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{santōṣam} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{வாழ்த்து}}
\textbf{\ta{வாழ்த்து}} (\emph{vāḻttu}) — \textquotedblleft{}a good wish\textquotedblright{}.

Straight off \emph{vāḻ}, 'to live, to flourish', which you had early. To give somebody a \emph{vāḻttu} is to wish them a life — not luck, not success, but the thing itself.

\emph{vāḻttukkaḷ} is what a Tamil speaker says where English says \textquotedblleft{}congratulations\textquotedblright{}, and it is the kinder sentence of the two: flourishing, offered in the plural, rather than a nod at what you managed to pull off.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four, and the fourth one is given rather than felt.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{vāḻttu}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{santōṣam}, then \emph{vāḻttu}, and feel the \ta{ழ} glide in the second
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{வாழ்த்து} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a good wish\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[mikka naṉṟi]{\ta{மிக்க} \ta{நன்றி} (mikka naṉṟi) — thank you very much}

\label{lesson:TA-C49-many-thanks}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{vāḻttu} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{மிக்க} \ta{நன்றி}}
\textbf{\ta{மிக்க} \ta{நன்றி}} (\emph{mikka naṉṟi}) — \textquotedblleft{}thank you very much\textquotedblright{}.

\emph{naṉṟi} has been with you since the very beginning. \emph{mikka} is the new piece in front of it: from \emph{migu}, 'to exceed', so it means abundant, more than the usual measure.

Tamil does not raise its voice to be warm. It puts \emph{mikka} at the front and leaves everything else exactly where it was. Set this beside \emph{tayavu seytu} and \emph{maṉṉikkavum} and the courtesy kit is complete.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
That closes the run: affection, respect, gladness, a good wish, and thanks with weight behind it.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{mikka naṉṟi}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item all five in order — \emph{aṉbu}, \emph{mariyādai}, \emph{santōṣam}, \emph{vāḻttu}, \emph{mikka naṉṟi}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{மிக்க} \ta{நன்றி} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}thank you very much\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
